rationale: The quality leg (revenue per unit of act+lct) is a genuinely different channel — capital productivity rather than cash coverage or cash conversion — from the many prior che/market interactions, though it is the Nth instance of the same template and the "working-capital base" is really a crude scale proxy (assets *plus* liabilities) rather than net working capital, so the economic interpretation is looser than the hypothesis claims.

This is a cosmetic variant of the archived "Cash-Conversion-Floor Cash Discount" — identical value leg and identical quality ratio oancf/(act+lct), with TS_MIN swapped for NEG(VOL) — and since a 3-period minimum already largely encodes downside stability, the two will be highly correlated and this adds little independent information.

Internally consistent and well-motivated (the ABS(ebitda)+cogs scaling correctly avoids sign flips), but it is a mechanical recombination of two archived signals — "Cost-Scaled Cash Conversion EBITDA Yield" with the TS_MIN transform borrowed from the cash-discount floor signal — so the expected marginal evidence over the existing pair is small.

This is the archived "Maintenance-Covered Earnings Yield" with a NEG(VOL) term of the *same* ratio appended via SUMRANK; the added stability component is correlated with the level term and will mainly cost coverage (3-year history on (oancf−dp)/lt), making it an incremental tweak rather than a substantively different mechanism.

The sign logic is internally consistent, but the dominant term — sales yield interacted with (negated) gross margin, signed negative — reduces to a rediscovery of gross-profit-to-market/gross profitability, and the level-vs-trend change to the archived "Two-Sided Sales Deterioration Trap" is a transform swap rather than a new economic channel.

The cleanest proposal here: expression matches the hypothesis, the sign is unambiguous, and the worst-of-three earnings coverage of current liabilities is a distinct dividend-sustainability conditioner not yet paired with payout yield in the archive (which tested only after-payout cash coverage and liability growth), though it does flirt with well-known payout-safety screens.
